newsitem.title: DUBAI: GOLF-HOSPITAL LEADS DESERT CLASSIC BY TWO SHOTS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-HOSPITAL LEADS DESERT CLASSIC BY TWO SHOTS.

text.p: Spaniard Domingo Hospital, using a putter given to him by Jose Maria Olazabal, fashioned a three-under-par 69 to take a two-shot halfway lead in the Dubai Desert Classic on Friday.
But the former commercial pilot insisted he could not win the tournament because he lacked vital experience.

"I don't think I can do it because there are a lot of mental things that I'll go through and I don't know how I'll react because I have not been there before," said Hospital, who has never led at the halfway stage of a European Tour event.
Olazabal, making his comeback after an 18-month absence, achieved his objective of making the halfway cut despite a triple bogey eight midway through his second round of 74.
The 38-year-old Hospital, a Tour player for just four years, scrambled through some bad driving by taking just 27 putts after switching on Tuesday to the club given him two years ago by Olazabal.
"I brought it with me just to practise with in my hotel room but after Monday when I putted badly with my old club I decided to use it," he said.
He needed only 28 putts on Thursday and one fewer in the second round.
"That's why I'm here talking to you," said Hospital after compiling a 36-hole total of 134, 10 under par..

The big-name challengers are lining up behind him. Ian Woosnam and Bernhard Langer, perennial Ryder Cup stalwarts, share second place on eight under after respective rounds of 67, the best score on a windy day, and 70.
Titleholder Colin Montgomerie is another shot back after a 72, with world number one Greg Norman in a group on five under after a 68.
Olazabal, out of action with chronic foot problems, drove badly at the 18th hole, his ninth, but battled back for a 74 that left him inside the cutoff of one over par.
"I'm happy just to be playing at the weekend," he said.

However, Seve Ballesteros soared to an 84 and at 14 over par the 1992 winner here missed the halfway cut for the third time in his three events this year. Only two players in the 130-man field, one an amateur, had higher totals.
Hospital's round included an eagle three at the 550-yard 13th where he chipped in from just off the green 20 feet away.
"It was mainly a scrambling round. I chipped and putted a lot of times for par. I missed all the fairways and all the greens but I was lucky with the putter," he said.
Woosnam, who won four titles last year, made five putts of between eight and 30 feet for birdies in his round to boost his chance of a first win in 1997.
It was a welcome improvement in his putting. "I just tried standing a little closer to the ball with my eyes over the top a little more and using my shoulders a little more," he said.
Langer, a convert to the broomhandle putter after problems on the greens last year, reaped the benefits in a morning wind that made scoring difficult.
Norman, also making a comeback after three months away from tournaments, was delighted with his birdies on the tough par-four eighth and ninth holes, the two hardest on the course.
"I hit drive and three iron to both greens and holed putts of 18 and 20 feet. I hit six beautiful shots there," he said.
